name: POPE
description: A polling-based object probing evaluation dataset/pipeline for evaluating object hallucination in large vision-language models, constructed from image datasets by pairing images with Yes/No questions about ground-truth and nonexistent objects.
creator: Yifan Li, Yifan Du, Kun Zhou, Jinpeng Wang, Wayne Xin Zhao, Ji-Rong Wen
citeAs: Li, Yifan; Du, Yifan; Zhou, Kun; Wang, Jinpeng; Zhao, Wayne Xin; Wen, Ji-Rong. Evaluating Object Hallucination in Large Vision-Language Models. arXiv:2305.10355v3.
rai:dataCollection: POPE is constructed from image caption datasets by first obtaining objects in each image either from human annotations or automatic segmentation tools like SEEM, then building polling questions using ground-truth objects and sampled nonexistent objects. The paper evaluates POPE on the validation sets of MSCOCO, A-OKVQA, and GQA. For MSCOCO, the authors randomly select 500 images with more than 3 ground-truth objects in the annotations and construct 6 questions for each image, with a 1:1 ratio between ground-truth and nonexistent objects for label balance.
rai:dataCollectionType: Secondary Data analysis, Document analysis, Software Collection
rai:dataCollectionRawData: Input images and object annotations from existing datasets, primarily MSCOCO, and additionally A-OKVQA and GQA. Ground-truth objects are taken from human annotations when available, or from automatic segmentation results produced by SEEM for unannotated settings.
rai:dataManipulationProtocol: After obtaining image objects, the method constructs triples consisting of an image, multiple questions, and Yes/No answers. Questions with answer "Yes" are built from ground-truth objects. Questions with answer "No" are built by sampling nonexistent objects under three strategies: Random sampling, Popular sampling using top-k most frequent objects in the dataset that do not exist in the current image, and Adversarial sampling using top-k co-occurring objects with the ground-truth objects that do not exist in the image.
rai:dataPreprocessingProtocol: For CHAIR evaluation on MSCOCO, the paper follows prior settings that only consider 80 objects appearing in the MSCOCO segmentation challenge. For POPE on MSCOCO, the authors randomly select 500 images with more than 3 ground-truth objects and construct 6 questions per image. In SEEM-based settings, images from MSCOCO, A-OKVQA, and GQA are automatically annotated using SEEM before question construction.
rai:dataAnnotationProtocol: Annotations for POPE consist of binary Yes/No labels for object-presence questions. Ground-truth objects in the image are obtained either from existing human annotations in the source datasets or from automatic segmentation with SEEM. Questions are formulated using the template "Is there a/an <object> in the image?" and answers are assigned as "Yes" for ground-truth objects and "No" for sampled nonexistent objects.
rai:dataAnnotationAnalysis: The paper analyzes stability by comparing prompt variants and reports that POPE has lower standard deviation than CHAIR. It also analyzes consistency between POPE responses and generated captions: for InstructBLIP and MiniGPT-4, objects receiving "No" responses were almost never mentioned in captions, and objects mentioned in captions usually received "Yes" responses. The paper also notes that when using automatic segmentation, label sets may differ from human annotations, causing divergence in evaluation results.
rai:dataSocialImpact: The paper states that object hallucination hinders the safe use of large vision-language models in real-world deployment and may result in unexpected consequences. It gives the example that an autonomous driving system could make wrong decisions when encountering unexpected events due to incorrect understanding of the external environment, potentially leading to serious safety issues. The authors hope the work can help develop more reliable and human-aligned LVLMs.
rai:dataBiases: The paper empirically reveals that object distributions in visual instruction data affect hallucination: LVLMs are prone to hallucinate frequently appearing objects in the visual instruction datasets and objects that frequently co-occur with ground-truth objects in the image. It also notes that visual instruction datasets are mostly constructed based on MSCOCO and share an unbalanced object distribution where top frequent objects occupy a major part of the dataset.
rai:dataLimitations: The work only focuses on object hallucination and does not measure overall LVLM capability. Due to computation limits, models are evaluated on only part of each validation set, so results may be affected by data distribution. POPE uses a matching-based method to determine whether models answer "Yes" or "No", and models may fail to provide answers explicitly containing these words, causing inaccurate evaluation. When combined with automatic segmentation, object labels may be inconsistent with human annotations, leading to divergence in results. The study also compares only a small number of LVLMs and excludes some recently released or closed-source models.
rai:dataUseCases: The dataset/pipeline is intended for evaluation of object hallucination in large vision-language models. It is used to benchmark models under Random, Popular, and Adversarial settings on MSCOCO, A-OKVQA, and GQA, and to study the relationship between hallucination and performance on VQA and image captioning tasks.
